label: Real run on this Mac's Docker Compose stack, with synthetic traffic from klaxon.traffic: synthetic data, a simulated provider, no real money. One fault from klaxon.faults, pool-exhaustion, was injected on purpose. The alert was raised by klaxon.alerts from what the stack showed. Klaxon's loop ran live on it, through Claude Code on Aravind's seat, offered one write action (rollback_deploy), which runs only if a person approves it at the gate, and stopped on diagnosed after 9 steps; any reply it got is a recorded response, not a simulation. The diagnosis was compared with the fault's recorded cause by a rule (klaxon.grading), not by a person or a model. Klaxon asked at the approval gate to act on its diagnosis; the request was approved with make approve (the request's id typed at a terminal), and the action ran: redeploy payments-api: PROVIDER_BREAKER on (unchanged), CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT cents (unchanged), REFUND_CONNECTION kept -> returned. Code, not the model, then verified it (klaxon.agent.verify): passed; the cause is removed, and the money is right. The fault's cause was removed by Klaxon: its rollback (Klaxon, approved request r-7b9d) removed the cause, and the harness's clearing then found the good settings running, and changed nothing.

fault.name: pool-exhaustion
fault.title: Payments fail: the payments API's database pool runs dry
fault.cause: a deploy of the payments API with a connection leak (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept): reading a payment's refunds takes a connection from its database pool of 10 and never gives it back, so after about ten refunds the pool is empty, and every request waits for a connection until the pool's 5 s timeout, then fails with a 500
expected_symptoms: the pool runs dry about 40 to 50 s after the deploy; then POST /payments takes 5 to 8 s (a worker thread, then the pool's 5 s wait) and fails with a 500: the p95 latency passes 7 s, and the 5xx share passes 70% within a minute
the payments API logs 'unhandled error' with PoolTimeout: no connection within 5 s
its health check fails too, so docker marks it unhealthy, while PostgreSQL itself is up
the traffic's clients retry and give up: many payments end with their outcome unknown, and arrivals past 64 in flight are shed
the money check passes: a payment that never got a connection was never charged, and one charged before its answer was lost is confirmed by its webhook
fault.remedy: roll the payments API back to REFUND_CONNECTION=returned: its new container starts with a full pool

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api was redeployed at 03:06:42 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. Under that setting, each refund request most likely keeps its Postgres connection instead of returning it to the pool. Refunds have arrived at about 0.1-0.4/s since about 03:06, so the held connections build up. Within about 30 s the psycopg pool is empty. From then on every request that needs the database, POST /payments and refunds alike, waits for the pool's 5 s acquire timeout and fails with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout as HTTP 500. That raised p95 for POST /payments from about 24 ms to 7.3 s. Provider calls stay fast, so the provider is not the cause. Traffic on POST /payments also grew, from 0.5/s to 5.8/s, which adds pressure on the pool, but the timeouts start after the deploy and after refunds begin.

evidence.shows: Confirms the alert: payments-api p95 was 0.02-0.5 s, then 7.33 s at 03:07:34.
payments-api was redeployed at 03:06:42, about 50 s before the spike, with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents. All other services were last created at 03:05:08.
payments-api's calls to the provider stay at about 5 ms p95 throughout, so the provider is not the cause.
Slow POST /payments requests since 03:06:58 all last almost exactly 5.0 s, the length of a fixed timeout.
One slow request has no database or provider span. It ends with HTTP 500 and error.type psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout after 5003 ms: it waited 5 s for a Postgres connection and got none.
payments-api ERROR logs are a steady stream of PoolTimeout exceptions on POST /payments.
Refund requests began at about 03:05:50 and continued at 0.1-0.4/s. POST /payments traffic rose from 0.5/s to 5.8/s.
Successful refund latency creeps up after 03:06:56. From 03:07:11, both /payments and refunds return 500s at about 7.4 s p95, so every route that needs a database connection fails: the pool is empty.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 03:06:42 deploy, presumably a REFUND_CONNECTION value that releases the connection after each refund. Recreating the container also frees the held connections. Afterwards, confirm that PoolTimeout errors stop and that p95 for POST /payments returns to about 25 ms. Then run money_check to see whether payments or refunds that failed with 500 left our books out of step with the provider.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, so in-flight payment and refund requests fail and clients must retry; idempotency keys in Redis should make retries safe. The rollback restores all of the earlier settings, including PROVIDER_BREAKER and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT, whose earlier values are not visible here. If one of them differed, for example the charge amount unit, the rollback could change charge behaviour. Check the deploy log before approving.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: If the earlier settings behave worse, recreate payments-api with the 03:06:42 settings (REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents). To stop pool exhaustion meanwhile, block or lower refund traffic, or raise the pool size, and restart the service periodically.
